module_title: Acquisition of Easements, Prescription, and Section 49 Rule
introduction: This intermediate tier explores how easements are legally acquired over time, the strict timelines for registering documents, and the severe legal consequences of failing to register a document that requires it.

core_concepts.title: Types of Easements (Section 5)
core_concepts.description:
1. Continuous vs. Discontinuous: A continuous easement can be enjoyed without human intervention (e.g., a right to receive sunlight through a window). A discontinuous easement needs a human act (e.g., a right of way/walking path).
2. Apparent vs. Non-Apparent: An apparent easement shows some permanent sign of its existence (e.g., a visible water drain). A non-apparent easement leaves no visible sign (e.g., a right to prevent a neighbor from building above a certain height).

core_concepts.title: Acquisition by Prescription (Section 15, Easements Act)
core_concepts.description:
You can acquire a legal easement simply by using someone's land for a long time without their permission.
- The Rule: The right must be enjoyed peaceably, openly, as of right (without asking permission), and without interruption.
- The Timeline: For private property, it must be enjoyed for **20 years**. For government property, it must be enjoyed for **30 years**. The suit to claim this right must be filed within 2 years of the 20/30 year period ending.

core_concepts.title: Time for Presenting Documents (Section 23, Registration Act)
core_concepts.description: A document (other than a Will) must be presented for registration within **4 months** from the date of its execution (signing). If you miss this deadline due to urgent necessity or unavoidable accident, the Registrar can grant an extension of another 4 months on payment of a fine (Section 25).

core_concepts.title: Effect of Non-Registration (Section 49, Registration Act)
core_concepts.description:
What happens if you buy land worth Rs. 50 Lakhs, sign the sale deed, but fail to register it?
- The Rule: Section 49 is brutal. If a document required to be registered under Section 17 is not registered, it shall: (1) NOT affect any immovable property comprised therein, (2) NOT confer any power to adopt, and (3) **NOT be received as evidence** of any transaction affecting such property. Legally, the sale never happened.

important_entities.name: Collateral Purpose Exception (Section 49 Proviso)
important_entities.key_fact: An unregistered document is not completely useless.
important_entities.significance: Even if an unregistered sale deed cannot be used to prove *ownership* (transfer of title), the court allows it to be used as evidence for a 'collateral transaction'—for example, to prove the *nature of possession* (that the person entered the property as a buyer, not a trespasser), or to prove a separate personal agreement not affecting the land.

trap_alerts_and_exceptions.explanation: Examiners will trick you by saying A used B's path for 25 years, but then A stopped using it for 3 years before filing the suit. Does A get the easement? **NO**. The law explicitly states the 20-year period must be continuous and must end *within 2 years* before the institution of the suit. By waiting 3 years to sue, A lost the prescriptive right.

mnemonics_and_tricks.explanation: Remember the differing timelines for claiming an easement over private land vs. government land.

exam_strategy_tips: If a Judiciary question asks 'Within what time period must a document be presented for registration after execution?', unconditionally select **4 months (Sec 23)**.
